# iters

```go
import "carswell.tech/x/iters"
```

Package iters provides lazy, composable operations over Go 1.23\+ range\-over\-func iterators.

[Seq](<#Seq>) and [Seq2](<#Seq2>) are locally\-defined types with underlying types identical to [iter.Seq](<https://pkg.go.dev/iter/#Seq>) and [iter.Seq2](<https://pkg.go.dev/iter/#Seq2>) respectively. They exist so this package can attach methods to them \(Go does not allow adding methods to types declared in another package, including generic instantiations of stdlib types\). Because Seq and Seq2 are distinct named types from iter.Seq and iter.Seq2, passing a value between the two — e.g. into or out of a stdlib function like slices.Collect or maps.Keys — requires an explicit conversion such as iter.Seq\[T\]\(mySeq\) or Seq\[T\]\(stdSeq\); Go does not convert between named types with identical underlying types implicitly. Range\-over\-func itself does not require any conversion: "for v := range mySeq" works directly, since the range\-over\-func spec matches on the core type of the range expression, not its named type.

Almost every operation in this package is lazy and composes by wrapping the source sequence in a new function: nothing runs until the resulting Seq or Seq2 is actually ranged over \(directly, or via Pull/Pull2, ForEach, Reduce, Collect, Sink, Count, and so on\). When a consumer stops iterating early — by returning false from a yield function, or by "break"\-ing out of a "for range" loop — that early stop propagates back through every operation in the chain to the original source, so no unnecessary work happens beyond the last element actually consumed. The exceptions are [Reverse](<#Reverse>) and [Sort](<#Sort>), which must fully drain their source up front — see their doc comments for why laziness isn't possible there.

The operations provided are:

- [Filter](<#Filter>) / [Filter2](<#Filter2>): keep only elements matching a predicate.
- [Limit](<#Limit>) / [Limit2](<#Limit2>): truncate a sequence to at most a given number of elements.
- [Monitor](<#Monitor>) / [Monitor2](<#Monitor2>): stop a sequence early once a context.Context is done.
- [Map](<#Map>) / [Map2](<#Map2>): transform each element \(and, for Map2, its type\) via a function.
- [Expand](<#Expand>) / [Expand2](<#Expand2>): map each element to a sub\-sequence and flatten the results \(flat\-map\).
- [Reverse](<#Reverse>): reverse element order \(not lazy — see its doc comment\).
- [Sort](<#Sort>) \(with [DefaultSortFunc](<#DefaultSortFunc>) for the common ascending case\): sort element order \(not lazy — see its doc comment\).
- [Coalesce](<#Coalesce>): fold each Seq2 pair into a single value, producing a Seq.
- [Reduce](<#Reduce>) / [Reduce2](<#Reduce2>) \(with [Sum](<#Sum>) as a ready\-made summing [ReduceFunc](<#ReduceFunc>)\): fold a sequence into a single accumulated value.
- [ForEach](<#ForEach>) / [ForEach2](<#ForEach2>): invoke a callback for every element, for side effects.
- [Sink](<#Sink>) / [Sink2](<#Sink2>): fully drain a sequence without collecting anything.
- [Count](<#Count>) / [Count2](<#Count2>) \(via [Seq.Count](<#Seq.Count>) / [Seq2.Count](<#Seq2.Count>)\): count the elements.
- [Seq.Collect](<#Seq.Collect>): collect a Seq into a \[\]T, via the stdlib's slices.Collect.
- [Values](<#Values>): build a Seq from a \[\]T. [Unslice](<#Unslice>): build a Seq2 of \(index, value\) pairs from a \[\]T. [Unmap](<#Unmap>): build a Seq2 from a map\[K\]V.
- [Create](<#Create>): build a Seq directly from a variadic argument list.
- [Stringify](<#Stringify>) / [Join](<#Join>): convert a Seq\[T\] to strings and concatenate them.
- [ToChan](<#ToChan>) \(via [Seq.ToChan](<#Seq.ToChan>)\): drain a Seq onto a channel from a goroutine.
- [Pull](<#Pull>) / [Pull2](<#Pull2>): convert a Seq/Seq2 into an explicit next/stop pull\-style iterator, via the stdlib's iter.Pull/iter.Pull2.

<a name="Coalesce"></a>
## func [Coalesce](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/coalesce.go#L12>)

```go
func Coalesce[K any, V any, T any](f CoalesceFunc[K, V, T]) func(Seq2[K, V]) Seq[T]
```

Coalesce returns a function that lazily collapses a Seq2\[K, V\] into a Seq\[T\] by applying f to every \(key, value\) pair. Coalescing is lazy: no work happens until the returned Seq is ranged over, and stopping consumption early stops the source seq as well.

<a name="Expand"></a>
## func [Expand](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/expand.go#L25>)

```go
func Expand[T any](f ExpandFunc[T]) func(Seq[T]) Seq[T]
```

Expand returns a function that lazily maps every element of a Seq\[T\] to a sub\-sequence via f, and flattens those sub\-sequences into a single Seq\[T\] \(also known as flat\-map\). Each sub\-sequence is fully consumed before f is called on the next source element, so sub\-sequences appear in the result in source order, each one contiguous.

Expansion is lazy: no work happens until the returned Seq is ranged over. Stopping consumption early — whether while still inside a sub\-sequence or between them — stops both the current sub\-sequence and the outer source seq.

## func [Expand2](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/expand.go#L57>)

```go
func Expand2[K any, V any](f ExpandFunc2[K, V]) func(Seq2[K, V]) Seq2[K, V]
```

Expand2 returns a function that lazily maps every \(key, value\) pair of a Seq2\[K, V\] to a sub\-sequence via f, and flattens those sub\-sequences into a single Seq2\[K, V\] \(also known as flat\-map\). Each sub\-sequence is fully consumed before f is called on the next source pair, so sub\-sequences appear in the result in source order, each one contiguous.

Expansion is lazy: no work happens until the returned Seq2 is ranged over. Stopping consumption early — whether while still inside a sub\-sequence or between them — stops both the current sub\-sequence and the outer source seq.

<a name="Filter"></a>
## func [Filter](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/filter.go#L68>)

```go
func Filter[T any](f FilterFunc[T]) func(Seq[T]) Seq[T]
```

Filter returns a function that lazily filters a Seq\[T\], keeping only the elements for which f reports true. Filtering is lazy: no work happens until the returned Seq is ranged over, and stopping consumption early stops the source seq as well.

Whether T is a Wrapper\-shaped type \(as with \[Wrapper\] and \[Wrapper2\]\) is checked once, outside the loop, and if so, Filter also recovers any panic from f: rather than aborting iteration, it records the panic on the element's Error field and yields the element, so a single misbehaving predicate can't stop the rest of the sequence.


Filter2 returns a function that lazily filters a Seq2\[K, V\], keeping only the \(key, value\) pairs for which f reports true. Filtering is lazy: no work happens until the returned Seq2 is ranged over, and stopping consumption early stops the source seq as well.

<a name="ForEach"></a>
## func [ForEach](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/foreach.go#L17>)

```go
func ForEach[T any](f ForEachFunc[T]) func(Seq[T])
```

ForEach returns a function that fully consumes a Seq\[T\], calling f once for each element in order. Unlike [Filter](<#Filter>) or [Map](<#Map>), ForEach has no way to stop early — it always drains seq completely.

<a name="Limit"></a>
## func [Limit](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/limit.go#L15>)

```go
func Limit[T any](lim int) func(Seq[T]) Seq[T]
```

Limit returns a function that lazily truncates a Seq\[T\] to at most lim elements. If lim is zero or negative, the returned Seq yields nothing — seq is not pulled from at all. Limiting is lazy: no work happens until the returned Seq is ranged over, and — like [Filter](<#Filter>) and [Map](<#Map>) — a consumer stopping early stops the source seq too.

Limit never pulls more than lim elements from seq: it checks the limit again immediately after yielding the lim\-th element, so it does not need to pull a further element from seq just to discover the limit has been reached.

<a name="Limit2"></a>
## func [Limit2](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/limit.go#L51>)

```go
func Limit2[K any, V any](lim int) func(Seq2[K, V]) Seq2[K, V]
```

Limit2 returns a function that lazily truncates a Seq2\[K, V\] to at most lim \(key, value\) pairs. If lim is zero or negative, the returned Seq2 yields nothing — seq is not pulled from at all. Limiting is lazy: no work happens until the returned Seq2 is ranged over, and — like [Filter2](<#Filter2>) and [Map2](<#Map2>) — a consumer stopping early stops the source seq too.

Limit2 never pulls more than lim pairs from seq, for the same reason described in [Limit](<#Limit>)'s doc comment.


Map2 returns a function that lazily transforms every \(key, value\) pair of a Seq2\[K1, V1\] into a Seq2\[K2, V2\] via f, which may change both the key and value types. Mapping is lazy: no work happens until the returned Seq2 is ranged over, and stopping consumption early stops the source seq as well.

<a name="Monitor"></a>
## func [Monitor](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/context.go#L19>)

```go
func Monitor[T any](ctx context.Context) func(Seq[T]) Seq[T]
```

Monitor returns a function that lazily wraps a Seq\[T\] so that iteration stops early once ctx is done, in addition to stopping on the downstream consumer's own request. ctx is checked before each element is yielded, so an already\-done ctx stops iteration without producing that element. Like [Filter](<#Filter>) and [Map](<#Map>), stopping — for either reason — stops the source seq too.

Even if ctx is already done before iteration starts, Monitor still pulls one element from seq before it gets a chance to check ctx \(an unavoidable consequence of range\-over\-func: the first element must be produced before any loop body can run\), though that element is discarded rather than yielded downstream.

## func [Monitor2](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/context.go#L54>)

```go
func Monitor2[K, V any](ctx context.Context) func(Seq2[K, V]) Seq2[K, V]
```

Monitor2 returns a function that lazily wraps a Seq2\[K, V\] so that iteration stops early once ctx is done, in addition to stopping on the downstream consumer's own request. ctx is checked before each pair is yielded, so an already\-done ctx stops iteration without producing that pair. Like [Filter2](<#Filter2>) and [Map2](<#Map2>), stopping — for either reason — stops the source seq too.

Even if ctx is already done before iteration starts, Monitor2 still pulls one pair from seq before it gets a chance to check ctx, for the same reason described in [Monitor](<#Monitor>)'s doc comment.

<a name="Pull"></a>
## func [Pull](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/seq.go#L27>)

```go
func Pull[V any](seq Seq[V]) (next func() (V, bool), stop func())
```

Pull converts a Seq into a pull\-style iterator: repeated calls to next return successive values from seq, with ok false once the sequence is exhausted. stop must be called \(typically via defer\) once the caller is done pulling, even if the sequence was not fully consumed. Pull is a thin wrapper around the stdlib's iter.Pull.

<a name="Pull2"></a>
## func [Pull2](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/seq.go#L38>)

```go
func Pull2[K, V any](seq Seq2[K, V]) (next func() (K, V, bool), stop func())
```

Pull2 converts a Seq2 into a pull\-style iterator: repeated calls to next return successive \(key, value\) pairs from seq, with ok false once the sequence is exhausted. stop must be called \(typically via defer\) once the caller is done pulling, even if the sequence was not fully consumed. Pull2 is a thin wrapper around the stdlib's iter.Pull2.

<a name="Reduce"></a>
## func [Reduce](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/reduce.go#L20>)

```go
func Reduce[T any](f ReduceFunc[T]) func(Seq[T]) T
```

Reduce returns a function that folds a Seq\[T\] into a single T using f. The first element becomes the initial accumulator without calling f; every subsequent element is combined via res = f\(res, element\). If seq is empty, Reduce returns the zero value of T without calling f at all — there is no error for an empty input.

<a name="Reduce2"></a>
## func [Reduce2](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/reduce.go#L50>)

```go
func Reduce2[K any, V any](f ReduceFunc2[K, V]) func(Seq2[K, V]) V
```

Reduce2 returns a function that folds a Seq2\[K, V\] into a single V using f. The first pair's value becomes the initial accumulator without calling f; every subsequent pair is combined via res = f\(res, key, value\). If seq is empty, Reduce2 returns the zero value of V without calling f at all — there is no error for an empty input.

<a name="Sink"></a>
## func [Sink](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/sink.go#L8>)

```go
func Sink[T any](seq Seq[T])
```

Sink fully drains seq, discarding every element. It is useful for forcing a lazily\-built chain of operations \(e.g. [Filter](<#Filter>) or [Map](<#Map>)\) to run for their side effects alone.

<a name="Sort"></a>
## func [Sort](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/sort.go#L29>)

```go
func Sort[T cmp.Ordered](f SortFunc[T]) func(Seq[T]) Seq[T]
```

Sort returns a function that sorts a Seq\[T\] according to f \(see [DefaultSortFunc](<#DefaultSortFunc>) for the common ascending case\) and returns the result as a new Seq\[T\].

Like [Reverse](<#Reverse>), Sort is not lazy: sorting requires seeing every element first, so Sort fully drains its source \(via [Seq.Collect](<#Seq.Collect>)\) at the point it's called, not when the result is later ranged over.

<a name="Sum"></a>
## func [Sum](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/reduce_functions.go#L9>)

```go
func Sum[N constraints.Integer | constraints.Float](res N, el N) N
```

Sum is a [ReduceFunc](<#ReduceFunc>) that adds each element to the running total. Pass it to [Reduce](<#Reduce>) \(e.g. seq.Reduce\(iters.Sum\)\) to total a Seq\[N\] of any integer or float type. Per Reduce's rules, summing an empty sequence yields the zero value of N.

<a name="ToChan"></a>
## func [ToChan](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/chan.go#L8>)

```go
func ToChan[T any](seq Seq[T], buflen int) <-chan T
```

ToChan drains seq onto a new channel from a background goroutine, closing the channel once seq is exhausted. buflen sets the channel's buffer size \(0 for unbuffered\). The goroutine sends are paced by the channel: if the caller stops reading before the channel is closed, the goroutine blocks on its next send indefinitely.

## func [ToString](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/string.go#L22>)

```go
func ToString[T any](a T) string
```

ToString formats a as a string via fmt.Sprintf\("%v", a\). Values already of a string type, and values implementing fmt.Stringer, format as expected; anything else falls back to Go's default %v representation for that type.

<a name="Seq"></a>
## type [Seq](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/seq.go#L10>)

Seq is a single\-value iterator over sequences of T, with the same underlying function type as [iter.Seq](<https://pkg.go.dev/iter/#Seq>). It is defined locally so this package can attach methods to it; converting between Seq\[T\] and iter.Seq\[T\] requires an explicit conversion \(see the package doc comment\).

```go
type Seq[T any] iter.Seq[T]
```

<a name="Create"></a>
### func [Create](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/literal.go#L8>)

```go
func Create[T any](s ...T) Seq[T]
```

Create returns a Seq\[T\] that yields the given elements in order. It is the variadic\-literal counterpart to [Values](<#Values>), for building a sequence directly from arguments instead of an existing slice.

<a name="Reverse"></a>
### func [Reverse](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/reverse.go#L12>)

```go
func Reverse[T any](seq Seq[T]) Seq[T]
```

Reverse returns a Seq\[T\] yielding the elements of seq in reverse order.

Unlike the rest of this package's operations, Reverse is not lazy: since the last element can't be yielded until every earlier element has been seen, Reverse must fully drain seq \(via [Seq.Collect](<#Seq.Collect>)\) before it can return anything. This happens once, at the point Reverse is called, not when the result is later ranged over.

<a name="Stringify"></a>
### func [Stringify](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/string.go#L30>)

```go
func Stringify[T any](seq Seq[T]) Seq[string]
```

Stringify returns a Seq\[string\] with every element of seq converted via [ToString](<#ToString>). Stringifying is lazy: no work happens until the returned Seq is ranged over, and stopping consumption early stops the source seq as well.

<a name="Values"></a>
### func [Values](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/slice.go#L4>)

```go
func Values[T any](s []T) Seq[T]
```

Values returns a Seq\[T\] that yields the elements of s in order.

<a name="Seq[T].Collect"></a>
### func \(Seq\[T\]\) [Collect](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/collect.go#L10>)

```go
func (s Seq[T]) Collect() []T
```

Collect fully drains s into a new \[\]T, in iteration order. It is a thin wrapper around the stdlib's slices.Collect.

<a name="Seq[T].Count"></a>
### func \(Seq\[T\]\) [Count](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/iters/count.go#L16>)

```go
func (s Seq[T]) Count() int
```

Count fully drains s and returns the number of elements it yielded. It is equivalent to Count\(s\).


```go
func (s Seq[T]) Expand(f ExpandFunc[T]) Seq[T]
```

Expand returns a Seq\[T\] with every element of s expanded and flattened via f. It is equivalent to Expand\(f\)\(s\).


Filter returns a Seq\[T\] containing only the elements of s for which f reports true. It is equivalent to Filter\(f\)\(s\).


ForEach calls f once for each element of s, in order. It is equivalent to ForEach\(f\)\(s\).

Limit returns a Seq\[T\] containing at most the first lim elements of s. It is equivalent to Limit\[T\]\(lim\)\(s\).

Map returns a Seq\[T2\] with every element of s transformed by f. It is equivalent to Map\(f\)\(s\).

